entities.name: Antonio Malfante
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Antonio Malfante (d. 1450) was a pioneering Genoese merchant and explorer whose 1447 journey into the central Sahara, on behalf of the powerful Centurione Bank, represents one of the earliest documented direct European forays into the trans-Saharan trade networks of the medieval period. Operating from the port of Genoa, a pivotal maritime republic in the Mediterranean, Malfante's mission was to assess potential new routes for gold and other commodities, aiming to circumvent the growing Portuguese dominance over West African coastal trade. His detailed letter, written from Tuat in present-day Algeria, offers an invaluable firsthand account of the region's geography, economy, and cultural dynamics, making him a crucial figure in the history of European engagement with North and West Africa prior to the Age of Discovery.

Malfante's expedition in 1447 saw him travel deep into the oasis town of Tuat, a vital hub in the trans-Saharan trade routes linking the Maghreb with the empires of West Africa. His correspondence vividly describes the volume of gold, slaves, and other goods flowing through Tuat, as well as the intricate social structures and commercial practices of the local communities. He meticulously recorded observations on the political landscape, the nature of commerce, and the challenges of travel across the vast desert, providing concrete intelligence that was highly sought after by European mercantile houses eager to access the fabled gold of the Sudan without relying on intermediaries or Portuguese-controlled sea lanes.
